definitions.plain_definition: A way of studying God using the same careful methods scientists use to study nature.
The surprising fact that math, which humans made up in their heads, perfectly describes how the real world works.
definitions.used_in_context: Eugene Wigner called this 'the unreasonable effectiveness of mathematics in the natural sciences.'

definitions.plain_definition: The branch of philosophy that asks about the basic nature of reality, beyond what science can measure.
Basic beliefs you have to accept before you can even start doing science.
definitions.used_in_context: Every scientific enterprise rests on presuppositions that science itself cannot validate.

definitions.plain_definition: The idea that when you try to prove something, you end up in one of three dead ends: an endless chain of reasons, a circle, or just stopping at a belief you can't prove.
definitions.used_in_context: The Münchhausen Trilemma, formulated by Hans Albert, demonstrates that any attempt to justify knowledge leads to one of three unacceptable outcomes.

definitions.plain_definition: An endless chain of reasons where each reason needs another reason, going on forever.
An argument that uses its own conclusion as one of its premises, like saying 'the Bible is true because it says it is true.'
A basic assumption you just decide to accept without proof, even though you could have chosen a different one.
Basic starting assumptions that you accept as true without proof, like the rules of a game.
definitions.used_in_context: It simply stops at its axioms and gets on with the work.

definitions.plain_definition: Ideas about God that are taken as true, often based on religious belief.
A pattern that is both complicated and matches a specific meaning, like a sentence in a book, which suggests it was designed.
definitions.used_in_context: Complex specified information implies a designer.

definitions.plain_definition: The observation that the universe's basic settings (like the strength of gravity) are exactly right for life to exist, as if they were carefully chosen.
A pattern that is both complex (hard to produce by chance) and specified (matches a meaningful pattern), which is a sign of design.
definitions.used_in_context: each exhibits specified complexity that is not explained by chance or necessity.

definitions.plain_definition: When a system's parts combine to create new, unexpected properties that the parts don't have on their own, like wetness emerging from hydrogen and oxygen atoms.
When a system naturally arranges itself into a more ordered pattern without outside help, like snowflakes forming crystals.
The idea that our universe is just one of an infinite number of universes, each with different laws of physics.
definitions.used_in_context: If there are infinitely many universes, one will be fine-tuned by chance.

definitions.plain_definition: A perfect one-to-one matching between two different systems, where the structure of one is exactly the same as the structure of the other.
definitions.used_in_context: Not as analogy, but as isomorphism.

definitions.plain_definition: A similarity in the way two different things are organized or built.
A mathematical formula that tries to describe how moral goodness (coherence) increases or decreases over time in a society.
definitions.used_in_context: Theophysics proposes a formal equation for moral coherence

definitions.plain_definition: A type of math equation that describes how something changes over time, like how fast a population grows or a cup of coffee cools down.
definitions.used_in_context: a differential equation that describes how coherence evolves

definitions.plain_definition: The branch of physics that deals with heat, energy, and how order tends to turn into disorder.
definitions.used_in_context: It is derived from three independent domains: thermodynamics, population dynamics, and information theory.

definitions.plain_definition: The study of how populations of living things change in size and composition over time.
definitions.used_in_context: It is derived from three independent domains: thermodynamics, population dynamics, and information theory.

definitions.plain_definition: The mathematical study of how information is measured, stored, and communicated.
definitions.used_in_context: It is derived from three independent domains: thermodynamics, population dynamics, and information theory.

definitions.plain_definition: A measure of disorder or randomness in a system; in physics, it always increases over time.
The physical law that says disorder (entropy) in a closed system always increases over time; things naturally fall apart.
definitions.used_in_context: a formal statement of the Second Law applied to moral systems.

definitions.plain_definition: A computer program that checks mathematical proofs to make sure every step is logically correct.
definitions.used_in_context: This equation has been verified in Lean 4

definitions.plain_definition: Using a computer to check that a mathematical proof or logical argument has no mistakes.
The idea that the most basic, underlying layer of reality comes first and is more fundamental than what is built on top of it.
A main mathematical formula that describes how a system changes over time, often used in physics and chemistry.
In this framework, the force or action (like God's grace) that helps increase moral goodness (coherence) in a system.
A comparison between a famous physics theorem (Noether's theorem) and the Ten Commandments, suggesting both are about underlying laws that keep things stable.
Tests to check if the perfect one-to-one matching (isomorphism) between two systems actually holds up under scrutiny.
A test that tries to find flaws in an argument by seeing if other, false explanations can also pass the same tests.
definitions.used_in_context: The adversarial discriminator: false-positive controls fail the same gate

definitions.plain_definition: Tests that check if a method incorrectly identifies something as true when it is actually false.
definitions.used_in_context: false-positive controls fail the same gate

definitions.plain_definition: A Greek word meaning 'word,' 'reason,' or 'principle'; in Christian theology, it refers to Jesus Christ as the rational order behind the universe.
definitions.used_in_context: The Logos is not the top of the ladder. The Logos is the ground the ladder is standing on.

definitions.plain_definition: Having to do with the study of knowledge: how we know what we know.
Having to do with the study of being and existence: what it means for something to exist.
Able to be proven wrong by evidence; a key requirement for a scientific theory.
The principle that evidence from different, independent sources all points to the same conclusion.
A way of calculating how likely something is, based on prior knowledge and new evidence.
A philosophical argument that says the universe had a beginning, and therefore must have had a cause (God).
The idea that everything that begins to exist has a cause, and the first cause of the universe is God.
A single mathematical or logical system that can describe many different things in a consistent way.
The philosophical challenge of explaining why a good and powerful God would allow evil and suffering in the world.
definitions.used_in_context: the suffering problem is real and unresolved

definitions.plain_definition: An attempt to explain why a good God allows evil and suffering.
When multiple independent lines of evidence all lead to the same conclusion.
A measurable pattern in real-world data that indicates a particular cause or process is at work.
definitions.used_in_context: It is the empirical signature of what happens when the why is suppressed.

definitions.plain_definition: A computer program that helps mathematicians check their proofs for errors.
definitions.used_in_context: a formal proof assistant that checks every step for logical validity.

definitions.plain_definition: The property of an argument where if the premises are true, the conclusion must also be true, regardless of whether the premises actually are true.
definitions.used_in_context: a formal proof assistant that checks every step for logical validity.

definitions.plain_definition: A mathematical function that describes how something new is produced from existing elements.
definitions.used_in_context: G = Generative function (how order produces coherence)

definitions.plain_definition: Something that brings order to a system, like a law, a structure, or in this framework, grace.
The speed at which something breaks down or becomes less ordered.
